Deepak Agarwal crisp on financials. Credible given the stated 4-year over-delivery record.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
- **Solar model flipped capex→opex:** the "solar project" is now a 26% stake in a PE-backed JV (Emerge Green Power) built on buyback/warranty terms — minimal own-capex, captive-power cost benefit, non-RPT.

- Fundraise is pure optionality ("no such opportunity we are evaluating"), not a signalled deal.

- Stated tenets: "CAPEX funded by accruals; Debt only for working capital", "Capex phased to cash flows", "Debt-to-Equity capped at 0.5x", "Capital allocation: 70:20:10 Growth, Liquidity, Dividend", and "Start small, gain Industry insights, then commit larger capital".
- Net cash position at peak capex: Mar-26 gross debt Rs. 957 Cr, net debt Rs. (378) Cr, gross debt/equity 0.08 and net debt/EBITDA -0.16; the commitments slide shows FY26A "Net D/E: 0.07x, Zero net debt" versus a committed FY25 level, and the deck states "The company is cash positive even at peak CAPEX cycle".
- Dividend policy in practice: "Despite continuous incremental capex spends, the Company has paid post IPO dividend amounting to Rs. 714 crore being 11% of the aggregate PAT of Rs. 6,410 crore"; FY26 net profit Rs. 1,061 Cr with dividend Rs. 126 Cr and payout 12% (payout was 5%/11%/14%/12%/14%/12% across FY21-FY26).

(378) Cr to ~Rs. (732) Cr against gross debt rising from Rs. 957 Cr to ~Rs. 4,226 Cr. The growth-roadmap slide states the same FY31E targets as Rs. 42,647 Cr revenue and Rs. 6,236 Cr EBITDA.
- Funding constraint on the whole roadmap: "No new equity / No increase in Net Debt / CRISIL AA+ Stable - All five moves funded entirely from internal cash generation."
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- Integration — a single ownership structure connects ore beneficiation, captive power, intermediate processing and finished product manufacturing, embedding cost predictability and quality control across the chain
- Geography — all facilities sit within 250 km of India's mineral belts, proximate to national highways and deep-water ports (Haldia, Paradip, Dhamra, Visakhapatnam)
- Logistics — captive railway sidings at Sambalpur and Jamuria plus a fleet of 19 railway rakes give direct control over raw material inflow and product distribution
- Energy — approximately 81% of power is sourced captively (467 MW captive power), with an expanding green energy portfolio; CMD states over 80% of energy is generated internally, described as both a cost moat and a carbon hedge
- Diversification — seven product categories across four metal families reduce revenue concentration and cyclicality
- Self-funded growth — every expansion phase has been financed through internal accruals; the balance sheet is stated to remain net cash positive
- Track record — the Company has recorded a profit in every year since inception
- Land runway — 489 acres of the 1,827-acre land bank remain available for future expansion, avoiding greenfield land acquisition constraints
- Cost position in longs — for producers operating primarily in long products and value-added categories, as SMEL does, the FY26 pricing environment in carbon steel longs was comparatively more stable than in flats
- Waste-heat power generated at H2.0-2.5 per kWh (per the operations statement)
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Global steel pricing and import pressure (China) — Elevated steel exports from global markets, particularly China, and changing trade flows may create pricing pressure in domestic and international markets, affecting realisations and margins. Mitigation stated: product diversification, increased focus on value-added products, domestic market strength, disciplined cost management and integrated operations providing flexibility across product categories.
- Project execution and ramp-up risk on the largest capex programme in the Company's history — Large-scale capacity expansion, commissioning of new facilities and ramp-up of downstream projects may involve execution delays, stabilisation costs, lower initial utilisation and temporary margin pressure. This is structurally the sharpest risk because a Rs 10,155 crore programme with projects commissioning from FY29 sits ahead of the earnings it is meant to produce. Mitigation stated: phased capex execution, internal technical expertise, project monitoring, experienced operational teams, disciplined capital allocation and gradual ramp-up of new capacities.
- Raw material and energy cost volatility — Volatility in iron ore, coal, power, ferro alloy inputs, freight and other key costs may affect production economics, working capital requirements and profitability. Mitigation stated: integrated operations, captive power capabilities, strategic sourcing, inventory management, logistics infrastructure and cost-control initiatives.
- Financial risk from simultaneous large-scale expansion and input-price volatility — Large-scale expansion projects and volatility in raw material prices may impact cash flows, profitability and overall financial performance. Mitigation stated: strong liquidity position supported by healthy cash reserves and prudent capital management, strategic sourcing arrangements, long-term procurement contracts and disciplined capital allocation, alongside a demonstrated commitment not to breach the self-imposed 0.5x debt-to-equity ceiling.
- Market and competitive risk across steel, stainless steel and aluminium — Intensifying competition across the steel, stainless steel and aluminium segments may exert pressure on market share, pricing and margins — a risk that grows as the Company enters newer segments (stainless flats, wagons, battery-grade foil) where it is not the incumbent. Mitigation stated: product diversification, expansion of distribution channels and a growing focus on value-added and branded products.
- Environmental and regulatory risk, including GHG emissions and climate change — Evolving environmental regulations and compliance requirements may increase operating costs and necessitate modifications to production processes. The BRSR separately classifies GHG emissions and climate change as a RISK with negative financial implications, citing physical risks (extreme weather, resource shortages) and transition risks (evolving regulations, market changes, reputational harm). Mitigation stated: pollution-control systems, energy-efficient technologies, monitoring mechanisms, EHS governance, regulatory tracking, a 1.085 MWp solarization project, emission-control technology investment and adoption of electric vehicles.
- Supply chain risk / dependence on critical raw materials — Dependence on critical raw materials and potential disruptions in supply networks could impact production continuity and cost structures. Mitigation stated: integrated business model, captive power facilities, strategic inventory management and long-term supplier partnerships.
- Operational disruption and technology obsolescence — Delays in project execution, capacity expansion or operational disruptions may affect production efficiency, customer commitments and business growth plans; separately, rapid technological advancement may require continuous investment to maintain competitiveness and operational relevance. Mitigation stated: continuous investment in modern manufacturing technologies, process automation, supply chain optimisation, robust project management practices, and ongoing investment in advanced manufacturing capabilities, speciality products and research initiatives.
- Occupational health and safety (BRSR material issue, classified a Risk) — Failure to ensure a safe working environment can result in accidents, injuries or fatalities, leading to legal liabilities, operational setbacks and reputational harm; negative financial implications from worker compensation claims, legal action and reduced productivity. Mitigation stated: a comprehensive occupational health and safety management system across all facilities and work sites, aligned with ISO 45001 standards.
- Water and effluents (BRSR material issue, classified a Risk) — Failure to responsibly manage water resources can result in operational disruptions, regulatory non-compliance and reputational damage, with higher costs from water scarcity, wastewater treatment and regulatory compliance. Mitigation stated: monitoring and measurement of water consumption across all locations, promotion of recycled water, and Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) systems at all plants.
- Bribery and corruption exposure (BRSR material issue, classified a Risk) — Corruption poses legal and reputational risks and potential financial losses; inadequate anti-corruption measures leave the Company vulnerable to bribery, fraud and other unethical conduct, potentially leading to fines, penalties and loss of stakeholder trust. The Company reports an Anti-Corruption and Anti-Bribery Policy and a Whistle Blower Policy.

outlook.body:
- Transition from 'Ore to Metal' to 'Metal to Value' — shift the product mix decisively toward finished and value-added segments across four metal categories, with FY26 described as the year the shift became visible.
- Portfolio expansion principle: extend the value chain, never leave the integrated base — every new segment must leverage the integrated platform the Company already owns.
- Three-question capital allocation test applied to every project: does it leverage the integrated platform, does it carry a cost advantage from inception, and does the market offer a long structural runway; capital is allocated only when all three answers are yes (the discipline behind dropping the DI Pipe project).
- 'Proprietary Research to Value' methodology as the stated discipline behind every capital decision — exemplified by the stainless steel entry through Mittal Corp, which added downstream processing capability naturally backward-integrated with existing operations.
- Fund all expansion through internal accruals and keep the promoter stake undiluted.
- 70:20:10 capital allocation framework — 70% of surplus reinvested in growth, 20% retained as liquidity, 10% distributed to shareholders; stated to have operated consistently since listing.
- Sustainability as strategy — captive power infrastructure treated as both a cost moat and a carbon hedge; generating over 80% of energy internally positions the Company as a preferred supplier to customers with rigorous ESG requirements.
- Structural shift of the power mix toward waste heat recovery and green power to reduce purchased fuel dependency and lower generation cost, with a stated direction toward complete energy self-sufficiency.
- Circular manufacturing on the shop floor — washery rejects and process gases fuel captive power generation; Zero Liquid Discharge systems govern water management across facilities; emission reduction pursued through continuous process optimisation and technology upgrades.
- Deliberate technology selection for defined operational outcomes: CSP technology in the Hot Strip Mill (eliminates the intermediate reheating stage in HR coil production), Danieli rolling mill technology from Italy for stainless steel, and Achenbach technology from Germany for aluminium foil at EV battery-grade tolerances.
- Brand and channel deepening — the SEL Tiger brand is deepening presence across B2C and industrial channels; goal is to be the integrated metals partner of choice for customers valuing quality, supply reliability and product breadth from a single source.
- Export growth as aluminium foil reaches defence and packaging markets abroad.
- FY27-FY28 roadmap is about converting investment into steady-state performance rather than new commitments — stabilise the carbon steel projects commissioned in FY26, commission stainless steel and aluminium facilities, bring the wagon facility to production readiness, and add the Hot Strip Mill and SBQ projects.
- Invest in technical capability building, safety culture, leadership development and digital skills; workplace safety remains a priority across every facility.
- The Board has formulated and approved a Dividend Distribution Policy in terms of Regulation 43A of the SEBI Listing Regulations, setting out the parameters and circumstances the Board considers in determining distribution of dividend to shareholders and/or retaining profits earned; the policy is published on the Company's website and the FY26 dividend recommendation is stated to be in accordance with it. For FY26 the Board declared an interim dividend of 18% (H1.80 per equity share of H10 each) on 22nd July 2025, paid on 2nd August 2025, and recommended a final dividend of 27% (H2.70 per equity share of H10 each) on 11th May 2026 after evaluating the financial parameters of the Company, to be placed for shareholder approval at the 24th AGM (25th August 2026, via VC/OAVM). The Directors' Report states the Company does not propose to transfer any amount to reserves from surplus during the current financial year. A special resolution seeking fresh approval for raising of funds (under Sections 23, 42, 62, 71 and 179 of the Companies Act and the SEBI ICDR/Listing Regulations) is placed as special business at the AGM — an enabling authority rather than a stated intention to raise. Reinvestment philosophy stated elsewhere in the report is that every expansion is financed through internal accruals under a 70:20:10 framework (70% of surplus reinvested in growth, 20% retained as liquidity, 10% distributed to shareholders), with the promoter stake to remain undiluted.
- Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) systems are implemented at all plants to ensure thorough wastewater treatment in compliance with applicable standards; water consumption is monitored and measured across all locations and operations, and recycled water is promoted to reduce overall consumption.
- A solarization project with a capacity of 1.085 MWp is stated to reduce CO2 emissions by 12.5 lakh kilograms annually, alongside investments in emission-control technologies and adoption of electric vehicles.
- A comprehensive occupational health and safety management system is implemented across all facilities and work sites, aligned with ISO 45001 standards.
- BRSR is prepared on a Consolidated Basis (including Shyam Sel and Power Limited, Ramsarup Industries Limited and Shree Venkateshwara Electrocast Private Limited) with Reasonable Assurance of BRSR Core obtained from BDO India Services Private Limited.
- CSR is applicable under Section 135 of the Companies Act 2013; community programmes span livelihood and entrepreneurial pathways, scholarships, coaching centres and digital learning facilities, healthcare outreach and medical camps, water conservation, afforestation, renewable energy adoption, sustainable agriculture, sanitation, public infrastructure, sports promotion and preservation of local cultural heritage.
- Stated community-outcome metrics: 6 ponds revitalised, 1,00,000+ cattle supported, 5,000 meals served daily.
- Under Vision 2031 the growth programme is expected to generate over 10,000 new direct and indirect employment opportunities.
- Stakeholder grievance mechanisms are in place for every stakeholder group (communities, shareholders/investors, other stakeholders, employees and workers via the HR-One portal, value chain partners, customers, and others via the Whistle Blower Policy). In FY26, complaints filed were: communities 0, shareholders 19, other stakeholders 0, employees and workers 13, value chain partners 35, customers 38, others 0 — with ZERO complaints pending resolution at the close of the year in every category (FY25 comparatives: 0, 22, 0, 22, 22, 26, 12, also with zero pending).

- BRSR material responsible-business-conduct issues identified as OPPORTUNITIES: Environmental Impact Assessment; development and well-being of local communities; sustainability disclosures; environmental declaration of products; adoption of innovative, resource-efficient and low-carbon technologies and solutions; life cycle assessment of products and processes; sustainability in the supply chain.

outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: FY26 was described as a year in which the Company accelerated its platform build-out through capacity expansion, downstream integration and a sharper focus on value-added products, with growing presence in cold rolled products, stainless steel, aluminium foil, speciality steel and railway-linked applications. On the carbon steel side, the Pig Iron plant at Jamuria (commissioned in FY25) achieved 100% utilisation in FY26 and pig iron installed capacity rose from 0.77 MTPA in FY25 to 1.22 MTPA in FY26; colour-coated sheet capacity rose from 0.25 MTPA to 0.40 MTPA and the Colour-Coated facility reached 71% utilisation within its first full year. The greenfield Cold Rolling Mill at Jamuria, developed with an investment of C603 crore, commenced Phase 1 operations (2,50,000 TPA) in October 2024, with Phase 2 commencing operations in April 2026; CR coil and sheet emerged as a meaningful new revenue line in FY26 following commissioning of the mill. In stainless steel, the acquisition of Mittal Corp continues to provide the upstream billet and wire rod base, and a C1,800 crore downstream expansion at Sambalpur targets 6,00,000 TPA of finished capacity by Q1 FY29, which management says will turn the segment from a growth contributor into one of the Company's primary earnings anchors. In aluminium, capacity additions are being made under a C800 crore aluminium investment programme, and a planned extension into battery-grade aluminium foil aligned with India's electric-vehicle transition is stated to be in advanced development. Looking forward, the Chairman/JMD roadmap states that carbon steel projects commissioned during FY26 are stabilising, stainless steel and aluminium facilities are targeted for commissioning in the next 12-24 months, the wagon manufacturing facility is progressing toward production readiness, and the Hot Strip Mill and SBQ projects will further strengthen downstream integration, with FY2027-28 identified as the inflection point. At Kharagpur a new blast furnace and an advanced railway wagon manufacturing facility have been commissioned and an upcoming Special Bar Quality (SBQ) mill is planned. Financially, against a C16,086 crore capex plan, C8,630 crore has been incurred (53%), of which C6,136 crore is capitalised (38% of the total plan) and C2,494 crore sits in assets that are commissioning, ramping or approaching steady state; the Board has approved a fresh capex of C6,660 crore plus an additional C2,700 crore split between a C900 crore SBQ Mill and the C1,800 crore stainless steel expansion, both targeting March 2029, taking the aggregate programme over the next 3-4 years to approximately C10,155 crore funded entirely through internal accruals, with a C7,500 crore enabling resolution approved by shareholders and held as dry powder with no immediate utilisation plans. On the sustainability side, the BRSR states solar capex covering an existing floating solar DC capacity of 1.2 MWP (0.99 MW) and a proposed 3 MW rooftop project costing C10.5 crore, plus conversion of a Direct Chute Feeder to a Y Chute in the AFBC boiler; 18% of FY26 capex (FY25: 11%) was in technologies to improve environmental and social impacts. The physical runway for further expansion is 489 acres of the 1,827-acre land bank that remain available, with 1,338 acres under active operations across eight facilities in four states.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- India's economy growing at 7-8% annually, driven by sustained investment in infrastructure, railways, defence, clean energy and electric mobility; the demand profile for metals is shifting toward differentiated materials, specialised alloys and precision-manufactured products.
- Indian GDP growth projected at 6.8%-7.2% in FY27, driven by continued public capital expenditure, a recovery in private investment and stable consumption demand; infrastructure spending across railways, highways and industrial corridors will remain the primary driver of demand for steel-intensive sectors.
- Imposition of a 12% safeguard duty on certain flat steel products from April 2025 (confirmed as a three-year measure) plus anti-dumping duties on specific Chinese electrical steel improved pricing discipline and provided partial relief in H2 FY26; the January price correction confirmed the impact.
- Chinese overcapacity is the defining feature of the global landscape — Chinese steel exports rose to an all-time high of 119 million tonnes in CY25, compressing domestic Indian realisations through the first three quarters of FY26; China's steel demand is expected to decline a further 1-1.5% in CY26 with exports projected to remain above 100 million tonnes, so the supply overhang is expected to persist near term.
- FY26 growth came from volume gains, operating leverage from higher asset utilisation and an improving product mix rather than price — management states that growing earnings through a pricing downcycle shows the earnings growth is structural and 'will repeat'.
- Indian steel demand grew 7-8% domestically in FY26; crude steel production rose 10.7% to 168.4 million tonnes and finished steel consumption rose 7.6% to 163.7 million tonnes; India regained net exporter status with exports up 35.9% to 6.6 million tonnes.
- For producers operating primarily in long products and value-added categories, as Shyam Metalics does, the pricing environment in carbon steel longs was comparatively more stable than in flats, though not immune to broader realisation compression.
- Faster-growing adjacent segments relevant to the Company: stainless steel consumption rising on infrastructure, railways and consumer applications with domestic producers gaining share as anti-dumping investigations progress; speciality alloys demand growing on automotive, engineering and industrial applications; aluminium foil and downstream products benefiting from packaging, pharmaceuticals and renewable energy demand.
- Vertical integration supports merchant volumes and internal cost efficiency, since pig iron, sponge iron and ferro alloys serve as both saleable products and captive intermediates.
- Cost-intensive environment — India imports approximately 85-90% of its coking coal requirements and volatility in coking coal prices, energy expenses and freight rates continues to influence production economics; integrated producers with captive power and diversified revenue are structurally better positioned.
- Margin lever from capex maturation: 62% of capex has yet to reach the P&L, so management states the trajectory toward its return targets is embedded in the existing asset base — 'the earnings are a function of time, not additional spend'.
- Over the next 18-24 months, assets that are commissioning, ramping or approaching steady-state will begin contributing to revenue and EBITDA without requiring additional capital deployment.
- FY2027-28 is identified as the inflection point — the year the investments mature into steady-state operations and begin contributing meaningfully to overall manufacturing performance.
- WACC compression from the CRISIL upgrade to AA+ (Stable) described as a financial moat for a company deploying a large multi-year capex programme.
- Demand drivers cited by sector: infrastructure and construction (Indian construction sector USD 685 billion in 2025 to USD 1.25 trillion by 2034), automotive and transportation (premiumisation and EVs driving advanced high-strength and lightweight grades), engineering and manufacturing (USD 310.3 billion in 2025 growing at 9.1% CAGR through 2033), and renewable energy (283.5 GW non-fossil capacity as of March 2026 against a 500 GW by 2030 target).
- Low-carbon transition via renewable energy, waste heat recovery and energy-efficient technologies represents both a compliance imperative and a strengthening of competitive advantage for integrated producers with captive power already in place.

risks.note: Elevated steel exports from global markets, particularly China, and changing trade flows may create pricing pressure in domestic and international markets, affecting realisations and margins. Mitigation stated: product diversification, increased focus on value-added products, domestic market strength, disciplined cost management and integrated operations providing flexibility across product categories.
risks.risk: Global steel pricing and import pressure (China)

risks.note: Large-scale capacity expansion, commissioning of new facilities and ramp-up of downstream projects may involve execution delays, stabilisation costs, lower initial utilisation and temporary margin pressure. This is structurally the sharpest risk because a Rs 10,155 crore programme with projects commissioning from FY29 sits ahead of the earnings it is meant to produce. Mitigation stated: phased capex execution, internal technical expertise, project monitoring, experienced operational teams, disciplined capital allocation and gradual ramp-up of new capacities.
risks.risk: Project execution and ramp-up risk on the largest capex programme in the Company's history

risks.note: Volatility in iron ore, coal, power, ferro alloy inputs, freight and other key costs may affect production economics, working capital requirements and profitability. Mitigation stated: integrated operations, captive power capabilities, strategic sourcing, inventory management, logistics infrastructure and cost-control initiatives.
risks.risk: Raw material and energy cost volatility

risks.note: Large-scale expansion projects and volatility in raw material prices may impact cash flows, profitability and overall financial performance. Mitigation stated: strong liquidity position supported by healthy cash reserves and prudent capital management, strategic sourcing arrangements, long-term procurement contracts and disciplined capital allocation, alongside a demonstrated commitment not to breach the self-imposed 0.5x debt-to-equity ceiling.
risks.risk: Financial risk from simultaneous large-scale expansion and input-price volatility

risks.note: Intensifying competition across the steel, stainless steel and aluminium segments may exert pressure on market share, pricing and margins — a risk that grows as the Company enters newer segments (stainless flats, wagons, battery-grade foil) where it is not the incumbent. Mitigation stated: product diversification, expansion of distribution channels and a growing focus on value-added and branded products.
risks.risk: Market and competitive risk across steel, stainless steel and aluminium

risks.note: Evolving environmental regulations and compliance requirements may increase operating costs and necessitate modifications to production processes. The BRSR separately classifies GHG emissions and climate change as a RISK with negative financial implications, citing physical risks (extreme weather, resource shortages) and transition risks (evolving regulations, market changes, reputational harm). Mitigation stated: pollution-control systems, energy-efficient technologies, monitoring mechanisms, EHS governance, regulatory tracking, a 1.085 MWp solarization project, emission-control technology investment and adoption of electric vehicles.
risks.risk: Environmental and regulatory risk, including GHG emissions and climate change

risks.note: Dependence on critical raw materials and potential disruptions in supply networks could impact production continuity and cost structures. Mitigation stated: integrated business model, captive power facilities, strategic inventory management and long-term supplier partnerships.
risks.risk: Supply chain risk / dependence on critical raw materials

risks.note: Delays in project execution, capacity expansion or operational disruptions may affect production efficiency, customer commitments and business growth plans; separately, rapid technological advancement may require continuous investment to maintain competitiveness and operational relevance. Mitigation stated: continuous investment in modern manufacturing technologies, process automation, supply chain optimisation, robust project management practices, and ongoing investment in advanced manufacturing capabilities, speciality products and research initiatives.
